To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the isotopic composition in water of a leaf can be described by a model in which water is transpired from the sites of evaporative water loss, leaving heavier water to be transported further along the xylems and diffusively back to the sites of evapo-transpiration; and (2) the isotopic compositions of oxygen and carbon in the evolved gases can be predicted by the same model.

the isotopic composition in the transpired water is the same as the composition at the sites of water loss, which is the same as that of the mesophyll water, which is the average of that in the xylem at the sites of loss and the composition of the water entering the xylem.

(1) the isotopic composition at the sites of leaf transpiration is the same as at sites of leaf carbon assimilation, and (2) the isotopic enrichment of water in the leaf is a function of the spatial distribution of transpiration rate, and of the Péclet numbers in the radial and longitudinal directions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the enrichment of water isotopic composition in leaves.
the progressive enrichment of water in leaves as it travels from the roots to the stomata.
the progressive enrichment of oxygen isotopes in water along a leaf, and the effects of non-uniform transpiration rate on the average enrichment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the isotopic composition at the site of evaporation in a leaf depends only on the transpiration rate at that site and on the isotopic discrimination associated with the process of evaporation, but not on the transpiration rates elsewhere on the leaf, or on the isotopic compositions of water in the xylem or in the atmosphere.
the Craig-Gordon equation is valid for the average isotopic composition of the water transpired from a leaf with spatially uniform carbon isotope fractionation.

, if the isotopic composition is measured at sites where water is transpired, the isotopic composition will equal that of the water at the site of evaporation in mesophyll cells, averaged with transpiration rate weighting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the progressive enrichment along the transpiration path is a natural consequence of the spatial variation of transpiration rate.

the isotopic composition is determined primarily by the isotopic discrimination of the sites of water evaporation, and that the isotopic signature of the transpired water is determined by the spatial variation in transpiration rate.

the isotopic composition at the sites of water evaporation is determined by a modified Craig-Gordon model, while the isotopic composition for transpired water is determined by an area-weighted average of the isotopic composition along the leaf.
The main takeaway from our work is that

progressive enrichment along the length of a leaf is a robust prediction, and that this is a consequence of the transpiration-weighted averaging of isotopic composition that is required to predict average enrichment at the site of evaporation.
the isotopic composition in the transpiration stream is not the isotopic composition at the sites of transpiration, which is the composition of the mesophyll.
the isotopic composition at the site of evaporation is not the same as the average isotopic composition of the transpired water, and that the latter is not the same for all leaves of a plant.
